nameStory: The Common Whitetail gets its name from the mature male's distinctive chalky white abdomen that looks like a bright white tail when seen in flight. This white coloring comes from a waxy coating called pruinescence that develops as males age, making them look like they've been dusted with powder.
description: The Common Whitetail is a medium-sized dragonfly that's one of New England's most recognizable species due to its striking appearance. Males have chunky white bodies about 2 inches long and translucent wings decorated with bold brownish-black bands that create a distinctive checkered pattern. Females look quite different with brown bodies and spotted wings, making them trickier to identify at first glance.

idTips.label: Male's white body
idTips.description: Mature males have a thick, chalky white abdomen that looks like it's been painted or dusted with flour - no other dragonfly in New England has this bright white coloring

idTips.label: Wing pattern
idTips.description: Both sexes have dark brownish-black bands across their clear wings, creating a bold checkered or banded appearance that's visible even when perched

idTips.label: Female markings
idTips.description: Female bodies are brown with distinctive white zigzag stripes running down the abdomen that look like lightning bolts when viewed from above

idTips.label: Chunky build
idTips.description: Both sexes have a stockier, more robust body than many other dragonflies - they look sturdy and compact rather than sleek

idTips.label: Perching behavior
idTips.description: Often seen resting on sticks, rocks, or even bare ground near water, returning to the same favorite perch repeatedly

habitat: Common Whitetails prefer still or slow-moving waters like ponds, marshes, quiet lake edges, and sluggish streams throughout New England's lower elevations. You'll find them in both natural wetlands and human-made water features like retention ponds and park lagoons. They avoid faster-flowing waters and higher mountain regions, preferring warmer, sun-exposed areas where they can easily patrol their territories.

seasonality.spring: Adults begin emerging in late spring, with males developing their characteristic white coloring as they mature through May and June.
seasonality.summer: Peak activity occurs during summer months when you'll see males aggressively patrolling waterside territories and females laying eggs. This is the best time to observe their distinctive markings and behaviors.
seasonality.fall: Activity continues into early fall but gradually decreases as temperatures drop. Late-season individuals may show wear on their wing patterns.
seasonality.winter: Adults die off with the first hard frosts, while nymphs remain active underwater, feeding and growing beneath the ice until next spring's emergence.

funFact: Male Common Whitetails are such aggressive territory defenders that they'll attack their own reflection in car windows and mirrors near water, mistaking it for a rival male invading their turf!
confusionNotes: Females are easily confused with female Twelve-spotted Skimmers, but Common Whitetail females are noticeably smaller with shorter bodies and white zigzag abdominal stripes (versus the Twelve-spotted's straight yellow stripes). Remember: "Whitetail zigzags, Twelve-spotted goes straight."
contextualKnowledge: Some field guides may list this species under the genus Libellula rather than Plathemis - both names refer to the same dragonfly. Scientists have been debating the proper classification since the 1800s, so don't be confused if you see both names used.
compareHints: The Common Whitetail is the only member of the Plathemis genus in New England, making it unique among our local dragonflies. Within the larger skimmer family, it's most similar to the Twelve-spotted Skimmer, but males are easily distinguished by their solid white bodies versus the Twelve-spotted's brown body with white wing spots.
